The equity market, as represented by the s&P 500, slid 8.2% from october 18th, to 1343 on November 16th, before recovering 3.5% to around 1391 currently. as would be expected, over the same dates, a flight to and then limited retreat from, safety pushed us 10 year Treasury yields down from 1.8310% to a low of 1.5840%, before a rise to 1.6745% at the time of writing. even gold was not immune from negative investor sentiment, not acting as a safe haven as it fell from the same start date from $1,752/oz (although it had been in excess of $1,795/oz in early october) to a low of $1,672/oz on November 5th, a fall of 4.6%. it is currently 3.6% higher at over $1,732/oz. Brent crude oil (although feeling some marginal impact from recent tensions in Gaza) fell 6.8% between october 18th and November 5th, to under $105/ bbl, before rebounding 5.5% to around $110.50/bbl now. Prices had been as high as $116/bbl earlier in october.

The base metals sector also followed similar pattern, as the market was sold from its highs through end-october/early November. copper three-month values retreated 8.7% from $8,220/tonne on october 18th to a low of $7,506/ tonne on November 9th, before recovering to around $7,717/tonne currently. aluminium three month prices slipped 6.4% from october 18th to an october 29th low of $1,887/tonne, and are now 3.8% higher at $1,958/tonne. Despite the improvement in metals prices, investors do not appear confident in an imminent and sustained move upwards. cFTc managed money positions in copper show that the net long that had existed since mid-september, was gradually wound down from mid-october, and by midNovember had moved into a net short position. recent signs of progress in reaching an agreement on the Greek bailout package, which would allow the release of €44 billion in funds, have helped to temper earlier investor pessimism. Furthermore, confidence has grown somewhat that the “fiscal cliff” faced by the united states could be avoided, whereby failing to halt the $600 billion in expiring tax cuts and government spending could lead to recession. however, the us has not yet turned the corner, as Fed chairman Ben Bernanke highlighted, saying that “the ability of the Fed to offset headwinds is not infinite” and that “in the worst-case scenario where the economy goes off the broad fiscal cliff...i don’t think the Fed has the tools to offset that.” still hopes that china will come to the rescue although sentiment over chinese growth prospects has been dialled down in recent months, there is growing consensus that the slowdown has bottomed out. ##### EcONOMic iNdicatORs revised oecD leading indicators show that the overall composite index has remained stable at 100.2 since july. of the major economies, the indicator for Germany has continued its downward trend, falling to 98.7 in september from 99.0 in august, although the overall eurozone indicator stayed at 99.4. china’s indicator has remained at 99.4 since june, while that for india has continued to decline, falling to 96.8 in september. october consumer confidence indicators reflect underlying regional trends in metals consumption. eurozone economic sentiment continued to fall, from 85.2 in september to 84.5. japanese consumer confidence declined from 40.4 to 39.8 in october. china, meanwhile, saw a surge in consumer confidence from 100.8 in september to 106.1. us confidence rose from 68.4 to 72.2 in october, which was likely helped by better-thanexpected recent non-farm payroll data and a slightly improved unemployment rate (+171,000 jobs and 7.9%, respectively). Purchasing managers’ indices were in line with consumer confidence in october. The eurozone Pmi fell from 46.1 to 45.4. however, the November result was released at the time of writing and showed a rebound to 46.2. The united states’ ism index rose slightly from 51.5 in september to 51.7. The New orders and Production components both helped to raise the index, whilst employment, Prices and imports were amongst the drags on manufacturing activity. china’s factory activity, which showed only a slight pickup in september, jumped from 47.9 to 49.5 in october and data just released for November saw a move back into expansionary territory, at 50.4, for the first time since october 2011. japan’s Pmi slid to 46.9 in october, from 48.0 the previous month. industrial output data for the eurozone in

september proved to be very negative, not only for the region as a whole, but for each of the highlighted major economies. overall iP fell by 2.5% on the month, which including drops of -1.8% for Germany, -2.7% for France, -1.5% for italy and -1.8% for the uK. us industrial production, which had recovered slightly in september, fell again, by 0.4%, in october. The Fed estimated that hurricane sandy cut output by almost 1 percentage point. The main impact on output was felt by utilities and by producers of chemicals, food, transportation equipment, and computers and electronic products. japan’s iP for august was revised lower from -1.3% to -1.6%, while september’s number fell by 4.1%. Thus suggests that falling exports (with weakness in europe being a major factor) and the territorial dispute with china are restricting capital expenditure. china’s industrial production posted a second consecutive month of gains, with year-on-year growth in october of 9.6%, providing some respite from gloomy data elsewhere. The industries driving this growth were textiles, chemicals, non-metal minerals, ferrous metals and transport equipment. adding further support were electricity and steel output. Third quarter chinese GDP was confirmed at 7.4% (as we indicated in last month’s report), but the iP trend suggests that this could be close to bottoming out. retail sales in china picked up to 14.5% in october from 14.2% the previous month, and above expectation. Fixed asset investment through october increased to 20.7% year-on-year from 20.5% over the first nine months of the year. inflation, meanwhile, edged lower to 1.7% from 1.9% in september, allowing some more room for economic manoeuvre. oecD leaDiNG iNDicaTor & Base meTals iNDeX ###### chiNese iP GroWTh & Base meTals iNDeX 105 Thomson Reuters GFMS 400

### ALUMINIUM ###### recent developments ###### outlook for the next twelve months **•** **_Prices have been under pressure since the second half of October as global economic prospects continue to falter and demand remains lacklustre. Consumers have focused more on destocking and next year’s requirements, adding to the damper market conditions. The ongoing growth in primary output and ongoing stock builds have been adding to the light metal’s market woes._** **•** **_Although LME stocks of aluminium have remained above 5 million tonnes since mid-September, they only recently took out the February record high, reaching a new all-time peak of 5.173 million tonnes on 19th November. Inventories at both Vlissingen and Detroit rema

in high (as do cancellations), with the latter seeing some hefty deliveries-in recently._** **•** **_Physical premium increases have shown some signs of slowing, and in the case of Japan, reversing, but not to a great extent. Availability of spot material remains restricted by the level of financed inventory, but consumer expectations of weaker market conditions have tempered demand in the short term. European premiums have firmed slightly, as consumer stock pipelines in the region remain tight, whilst premiums in the United States are flat to slightly lower. Slower auto exports and the dispute with China have helped Japanese premiums to fall more sharply._** **•** **_The aluminium market has so far in the fourth quarter underperformed versus our expectations. As such, we have revised lower our forecast prices for the quarter and hence for 2012 as a whole. We now expect average cash prices of $1,950/tonne and $2,006/tonne, respectively. For 2013, we expect prices to average $2,069/tonne._** **•** **_From a market balance perspective, we are still projecting that the market will remain in oversupply over the forecast period. We currently forecast market surpluses of 660,000 tonnes this year and 456,000 tonnes in 2013._** **•** **_A contango price structure is likely to remain in place for the foreseeable future, given the low interest rate environment outlined by the Fed and overall subdued demand helping to keep spot markets relatively weak. Thus, stock financing is likely to be a feature of the market for some time to come, in the absence of any regulatory changes. This should continue to keep premiums relatively firm, although support for underlying price is likely to be limited until there is a significant turnaround in consumption._** ###### thomson reuters Gfms’ forecast scenarIos **•** **_Chinese and US demand continues to outpace that in Europe and Japan and we are still expecting 4.7% global consumption growth this year. However, even though Chinese production estimates for October exhibited a slight dip, they still implied annualised production of 20.25 million tonnes. At the same time, the production rate for the rest of the world appears to have stabilised, following six consecutive months of decline._** **base Case, 45% Probability** represents what thomson reuters Gfms consider the most likely outcome for the markets. **Scenario b, 30% Probability** faster recovery than under our base case in the near term and stronger growth thereafter. **Scenario C, 25% Probability** the crisis in the eurozone spreads to cause a markedly slower recovery in the mature economies and a moderation in chinese growth. ###### alumInIum supply-demand balance and prIce forecast ###### Quarterly alumInIum prIce forecast |(000 tonnes)

###### market background following an lme week which focused less on underlying price, but more on warehouse queues and physical premiums, aluminium prices came under pressure for most of the second half of october, with a trough of $1,873/ tonne on a cash basis. prices have recovered since then, to current levels of around $1,950/tonne, but have been unable to gain further traction on the upside. as stocks continue to build on the lme, weak demand conditions have slowed the rise of premiums, and in the case of Japan, these have fallen. there are pockets of strength, such as the us automotive and aerospace markets, but these are not enough to carry the global market, especially as primary output (particularly in china) continues to grow. the chinese state reserve bureau (srb) has purchased an initial 100,000 tonnes (out of a planned 400,000 tonnes) of domestic aluminium as part of a programme to support the domestic market. however, it is likely that much more significant volumes would be needed to be taken out of the market to lift prices in any meaningful way. lme inventories reach new record high, as total reported stocks gain 5% for year to date lme stocks of aluminium have remained above the 5 million tonne level since mid-september, reaching a new all-time peak of 5.173 million tonnes on 19th november. there has been another increase in cancelled inventory, which now represents around 35% of total stocks and one of the most notable changes has been at detroit, where metal delivered-in has increased, while cancelled stocks have risen from around 40+% during september and october to around 56% currently. there have been knockon effects on potential offtake queues, which theoretically are now close to those at vlissingen. both locations now imply at least mid-august 2013 load-out dates for fresh cancellations. weekly chanGe In lme stocks vs spot prIce 150000 2200

market outlook the correction in prices that has materialised following the post-Qe3 bounce has been deeper than we envisaged and, with concerns over the global economy continuing to dampen prices of $1,960/tonne. looking ahead to next year, from a fundamental standpoint, zinc ranks amongst the worst in the base metals sector. indeed, we forecast the market to post a surplus of 276,000 tonnes
